pr_title: Make more Regex loops atomic automatically
pr_body:
For example, given an expression like "(abcd*)*e", the inner d* loop will now be converted to be atomic, e.g. "(abc(?>d*))*e)".  We're careful not to convert an expression like "(abca*)*e)", where the inner loop has no overlap with what comes immediately after the loop but does with the start of the loop.

I also fixed what appears to be a long-standing bug in how character classes are canonicalized.  An attempt was made to avoid running the canonlicalization routine, but we almost always need to do it, and we were not doing it in some cases, resulting in character classes that were correct but not as optimized as they should have been, e.g. two abutting ranges when one would suffice, leading to poorer code gen.  It's part of this PR because I caught when changing the reduction tests to validate the full code tree including strings rather than just the codes list.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/27402
cc: @danmosemsft, @eerhardt, @ViktorHofer

issue_context.title: some backtracking regexes slower on .NET
issue_context.body:
eg `(\w*)+\.` on `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa` takes a while:
 
BenchmarkDotNet=v0.12.0, OS=Windows 10.0.19041
Intel Core i7-7700 CPU 3.60GHz (Kaby Lake), 1 CPU, 8 logical and 4 physical cores
.NET Core SDK=5.0.100-alpha.1.20079.6
  [Host]     : .NET Core 5.0.0 (CoreCLR 5.0.20.7203, CoreFX 5.0.20.7203), X64 RyuJIT
  DefaultJob : .NET Core 5.0.0 (CoreCLR 5.0.20.7203, CoreFX 5.0.20.7203), X64 RyuJIT

|         Method |       Mean |    Error |    StdDev |
|--------------- |-----------:|---------:|----------:|
|          Bench | 2,593.0 ms | 51.76 ms | 131.75 ms |
| Bench_Compiled |   669.2 ms | 12.96 ms |  11.49 ms |

But on `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa` it takes substantially longer - minutes at least, even with `RegexOptions.Compiled`, using current master. I gave up waiting.

On this long text, where .NET is very slow, Rust is almost instant, PHP, Python and Golang are 100-300ms or so. Adding a period on the end to make it a match makes no difference.

Is there something we can do to optimize this pattern? I have no reason to believe it's an important one - I just reduced it from the disabled one in `Docs_Backtracking_LookaheadAssertions`

cc @stephentoub

review_comments: I assumed "descendent" was a spelling error, but apparently it's not. 😛
Well, maybe "recur" is a possible word to use, but "recurse" is more common. Either is fine I guess.
I had it drilled into me in college that "recur" is what happens when you employ recursion, and "recurse" is what happens when you swear again. Ever since "recurse" just sounds wrong to me.
For comments like this I'm mentally visualizing patterns, you might consider sprinkling more example patterns in comments.
I've gone through and added a lot of such comments.

Why is `#if DEBUG` required here? My understanding is that in release, `Debug.Assert` and everything that calls it is elided, and this includes any string interopolation being passed to it. Is that not the case?
The TypeName property is under an `#if DEBUG`.  In a release build, it's as if here this was `Debug.Assert(condition. $"{SomePropertyThatDoesntActuallyExist}")`, which doesn't compile.
ah yes
In this case, we're passing in the last child of the "concat" as the node, and the first child of the "concat" in as the subsequent. Maybe subsequent is not the right term then -- referent?
The idea is that we're testing it as if it's the subsequent node, e.g. with ab* testing what happens if it were b*a.

I think this is what I was thinking of when I opened the issue. 

Does this help a `(\w*)+` match succeed -- I assume that still runs interminably?

> Does this help a (\w*)+ match succeed

Yes. This doesn't eliminate all backtracking, but it changes `(\w*)+` to `((?>\w*))+`, which means that it won't backtrack into the `\w+`.  It'll still do a lot of backtracking, but also a lot less than it otherwise would.
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/31738/files#diff-2a526ef350bb57b99bc03248caae9d1dR328

Note that it doesn't help with the original expression off of which you based this, the one commented out in the tests.  That one has catastrophic backtracking, and there's little we can do about that; try it out on regex101 and you'll see the same terribleness with pcre.
A nested atomic to me means one atomic group inside another ? Like your `[InlineData("(?>(?>(?>(?:abc)*)))", "(?:abc)*")]`
I meant things nested inside an atomic that could/should themselves be made atomic.
I assume we have tests that hit this
I'll double-check and add tests to ensure we do.
this is guaranteed to never lead to a null `node` ?
Yes, a capture will always have a child.
